questions.question: What makes writing in a diary a strange experience for Anne Frank?
answer_steps: She had never written anything before.
She felt no one would be interested in the musings of a thirteen-year-old schoolgirl.

questions.question: Why does Anne want to keep a diary?
answer_steps: She wanted to write and get things off her chest.
She had no true friend to confide in, so the diary would be her friend.

questions.question: Why did Anne think she could confide more in her diary than in people?
answer_steps: Paper has more patience than people.
With people she could talk only about everyday things, not her deep feelings.

questions.question: Why does Anne provide a brief sketch about her family?
answer_steps: She treats Kitty as a friend who needs to know her.
No one would understand her stories without knowing her background.

questions.question: What tells you that Anne loved her grandmother?
answer_steps: She says no one knows how often she thinks of her and still loves her.
On her birthday a candle was lit for her grandmother.

questions.question: Why was Mr Keesing annoyed with Anne? What did he ask her to do?
answer_steps: She talked too much in class.
He asked her to write an essay titled 'A Chatterbox'.

questions.question: How did Anne justify her being a chatterbox in her essay?
answer_steps: She said talking is a student's trait.
She had inherited it from her mother, who talked as much, so it could not be cured.

questions.question: Do you think a diary is a good substitute for a friend? Why?
answer_steps: Partly: it listens patiently and keeps secrets, which helps to sort out feelings.
But it cannot reply, advise or comfort the way a real friend can.

questions.question: What made Mr Keesing allow Anne to talk in class?
answer_steps: Her funny poem 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterback'.
He took the joke well, read it aloud and stopped punishing her.

questions.question: Was Anne right when she said that the world would not be interested in the musings of a thirteen-year-old girl?
answer_steps: No, she was wrong.
Her diary became one of the most widely read books, read in many languages, because it shows a teenager's honest feelings during the Nazi persecution.

questions.question: Compare Anne's diary with ordinary diary entries. What language was the diary originally written in?
answer_steps: Ordinary entries list events and facts; Anne writes to 'Kitty' as to a friend, sharing feelings and thoughts.
The diary was originally written in Dutch.

questions.question: Why does Anne provide a brief sketch about her family? Does she treat 'Kitty' as an insider or an outsider?
answer_steps: She wants Kitty to know her before she shares her stories.
She treats Kitty as an insider, a close friend, though she begins by introducing herself.

questions.question: How does Anne feel about her father, her grandmother, Mrs Kuperus and Mr Keesing? What do these tell you about her?
answer_steps: She adores her father, loves and misses her grandmother, and is fond of Mrs Kuperus; she respects Mr Keesing after his change.
This shows she is loving, sensitive and fair-minded.

questions.question: What does Anne write in her first essay?
answer_steps: That talking is a student's trait and she would try to control it.
But she could never cure it, since she inherited it from her mother, who talked as much.

questions.question: Anne says teachers are most unpredictable. Is Mr Keesing unpredictable? How?
answer_steps: Yes. He punished her talkativeness with essays and seemed strict.
Yet he laughed at her arguments, took her poem as a joke, read it aloud and then allowed her to talk.

questions.question: What do these statements tell you about Anne: (i) 'We don't seem to be able to get any closer, and that's the problem.' (ii) 'I don't want to jot down the facts in this diary the way most people would.'
answer_steps: (i) She is introspective and lonely; she wants a deep friendship.
(ii) She is original and wants the diary to be a real friend, not a record of facts.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*Writing in a diary is a really strange experience for someone like me.*
*Not only because I've never written anything before, but also because it seems to me that later on*
*neither I nor anyone else will be interested in the musings of a thirteen-year-old schoolgirl.*

(i) Who is 'me' in the extract?

(ii) Why is writing a diary strange for her? (any one)

(iii) What does 'musings' mean?

(iv) How old was she?

(v) Was she right that no one would be interested?
answer_steps: (i) Anne Frank.
(ii) She has never written anything before.
(iii) Thoughts or reflections.
(iv) Thirteen.
(v) No; her diary became world-famous.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*'Paper has more patience than people.' I thought of this saying on one of those days when I was feeling a little depressed*
*and was sitting at home with my chin in my hands, bored and listless.*

(i) Who thought of this saying?

(ii) What does the saying mean?

(iii) How was she feeling that day?

(iv) Find a word meaning 'without energy'.

(v) What did this saying lead her to do?
answer_steps: (i) Anne Frank.
(ii) Paper listens patiently to anything you write.
(iii) A little depressed, bored and listless.
(iv) Listless.
(v) To keep a diary as her friend.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*Mr Keesing, the old fogey who teaches maths, was annoyed with me for ages because I talked so much.*
*After several warnings, he assigned me extra homework.*
*An essay on the subject, 'A Chatterbox'.*

(i) What does 'old fogey' mean?

(ii) Why was Mr Keesing annoyed?

(iii) What extra homework did he give?

(iv) What did Anne argue in it?

(v) How did Mr Keesing finally react?
answer_steps: (i) An old-fashioned person.
(ii) Anne talked too much in class.
(iii) An essay titled 'A Chatterbox'.
(iv) Talking is a student's trait, inherited from her mother.
(v) He took her poem as a joke and let her talk.

questions.question:
Read the extract and answer the questions.

*Mr Keesing was trying to play a joke on me with this ridiculous subject,*
*but I'd make sure the joke was on him.*

(i) Which 'ridiculous subject' is meant?

(ii) How did Anne make the joke 'on him'?

(iii) Who helped her write it?

(iv) What does this show about Anne?

(v) Give the opposite of 'ridiculous'.
answer_steps: (i) 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterback'.
(ii) She wrote a funny poem about ducks and a swan.
(iii) Her friend Sanne.
(iv) She is witty and confident.
(v) Sensible.

questions.question: Anne received the diary on:
questions.explanation: She was born on 12 June 1929.

questions.question: What name did Anne give her diary?
questions.explanation: She wanted it to be her friend.

questions.question: Where was Anne born?
questions.explanation: The family moved to Holland in 1933.

questions.question: Why did Anne's family emigrate to Holland?
options: because her father was a teacher there
questions.explanation: Anti-Jewish laws were starting in Germany in 1933.

questions.question: Anne's father became Managing Director of:
questions.explanation: The company made products used in making jam.
option_feedback: It was a company making jam products.

questions.question: When did Anne's grandmother die?
questions.explanation: A candle was lit for her on Anne's birthday.
option_feedback: That was the move to Holland.

questions.question: Who was the headmistress of Anne's Montessori school?
questions.explanation: Their farewell was tearful.
option_feedback: Mr Keesing was the maths teacher.

questions.question: What subject did Mr Keesing teach?
questions.explanation: Anne calls him 'the old fogey who teaches maths'.

questions.question: What was the title of the second essay?
options: Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterback
questions.explanation: Each title was meant to tease her.

questions.question: In the poem, what happened to the three baby ducklings?
options: their father bit them to death because they quacked too much
questions.explanation: The poem was a joke about chattering.
option_feedback: It is a comic poem about too much quacking.

questions.question: Who helped Anne write the poem?
questions.explanation: Sanne was good at poetry.

questions.question: Which quality of Anne is shown by her reply to Mr Keesing's punishments?
questions.explanation: She turned punishment into fun.
option_feedback: Her answers were clever, not rude.

questions.question: Anne's main problem with her friends was that:
options: she could not confide in them
questions.explanation: 'That's the root of the problem.'
option_feedback: She could not get close to them.
They were friends, just not close.

questions.question: 'Musings' means:
questions.explanation: The musings of a thirteen-year-old schoolgirl.

questions.question: How did Mr Keesing finally react?
options: he read the poem to the class and allowed Anne to talk
questions.explanation: He took the joke the right way.

questions.question: Who was Margot?
questions.explanation: She was born in 1926.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: Anne wanted to list facts in her diary like most people.
questions.explanation: She wanted the diary to be her friend, not a list of facts.
option_feedback: Not quite. She wanted the diary to be her friend, not a list of facts.
Correct! She wanted the diary to be her friend, not a list of facts.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: Anne's family was Jewish.
questions.explanation: That is why they left Germany in 1933.
option_feedback: Correct! That is why they left Germany in 1933.
Not quite. That is why they left Germany in 1933.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: Mr Keesing set Anne three essays as punishment for talking.
questions.explanation: A Chatterbox, An Incorrigible Chatterbox, and Quack, Quack, Quack.
option_feedback: Correct! A Chatterbox, An Incorrigible Chatterbox, and Quack, Quack, Quack.
Not quite. A Chatterbox, An Incorrigible Chatterbox, and Quack, Quack, Quack.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: Anne's diary was originally written in English.
questions.explanation: It was written in Dutch.
option_feedback: Not quite. It was written in Dutch.
Correct! It was written in Dutch.

questions.question: Describe Anne's relationship with her father.
answer_steps: She calls him 'the most adorable father I've ever seen'.
This shows her deep love and admiration for him.

questions.question: How did Anne turn the third punishment into a victory?
answer_steps: She wrote a funny poem with Sanne about a mother duck, a father swan and three chattering ducklings.
Mr Keesing laughed, read it aloud and never punished her again.

questions.question: Write a character sketch of Anne Frank based on the chapter.
answer_steps: Anne is thoughtful and honest: she looks into her own loneliness.
She is loving: she adores her father and lights a candle for her grandmother.
She is witty and confident: she answers Mr Keesing's punishments with clever arguments and a comic poem.
She is mature beyond her age: she writes with insight about people.
Her diary shows a lively teenager in dark times, which is why the world still reads it.
marking_scheme: 3 marks: content (relevant points from the text)

questions.question: 'Teachers are most unpredictable.' Discuss with reference to Mr Keesing.
answer_steps: Mr Keesing seemed strict: he was annoyed at Anne's talking and set her extra essays.
He kept raising the punishment with teasing titles.
But he laughed at her argument in the first essay, and accepted the duck poem as a joke.
He read it aloud and let her talk from then on.
His change from strictness to good humour shows he was unpredictable, and also fair.
marking_scheme: 3 marks: content (relevant points from the text)

questions.question: Imagine you are Anne. Write a diary entry to Kitty about the day Mr Keesing read your poem to the class.
answer_steps: Address: 'Dear Kitty' and the date.
Describe how you and Sanne wrote the duck poem.
Describe Mr Keesing reading it aloud and the class laughing.
Your feelings: relief and pride; he will now let you talk.
